html:
The devbox and Orca

Read this before step 0 of SETUP.md. Step 0 is yours, not your agent's: it needs your AWS account, sudo and the Orca app.

In plain words. A devbox is a Linux machine in the cloud (an AWS EC2 instance) that stays on while your laptop sleeps. The brain needs one. The dream, the Temporal server, the daily care agent and most long agent runs live there. Your laptop keeps its own copy of the brain and syncs with the devbox every hour. Laptop-only is not supported: without the devbox nothing files new memories, refreshes CARDs or checks the brain's health.

Orca is the multi-agent IDE you use on the laptop. On the devbox, Orca runs headless as orca serve, and the laptop's Orca app connects to it as a remote environment. Agents started there keep running when the laptop sleeps.

 LAPTOP (macOS)                                              DEVBOX (EC2, Ubuntu)
 ┌───────────────────────────────┐                         ┌──────────────────────────────────────────┐
 │ Orca app ── local runtime     │  ssh -L 16768:…:6768    │ orca serve :6768 (systemd --user)         │
 │   environment "<devbox>" ─────┼────────────────────────►│   └ agents in worktrees, keep running     │
 │ brain bridge 127.0.0.1:7722   │◄── ssh -R 7722 ─────────│ brain peer / agents note laptop:<name>    │
 │ brain sync (Unison) ──────────┼──── ssh ───────────────►│ /usr/bin/unison                           │
 │ browser ──────────────────────┼── ssh -L 8233 (on ask) ►│ Temporal UI 127.0.0.1:8233                 │
 │ scripts/devbox up|down|status ┼── AWS EC2 API ─────────►│ the instance itself                       │
 └───────────────────────────────┘                         │ /home/<devbox-user> ═ bind ═► /Users/<user>│
                                                           └──────────────────────────────────────────┘

Contents: 1 create the devbox · 2 the bind mount · 3 orca serve and pairing · 4 tunnels · 5 the devbox helper · 6 sign-ins · 7 security

1. Create the devbox

[HUMAN] You create the instance with your own AWS access, the way your team does.

Need Minimum Why
OS Ubuntu (24.04 LTS on the reference setup), x86_64 the release's Linux binaries are linux-amd64
CPU / RAM ≥ 8 vCPU, ≥ 32 GB Temporal, the worker, Orca and a few agents at once
Disk ≥ 200 GB gp3, DeleteOnTermination=false boxes, worktrees and results grow; the disk must outlive the instance
Address an Elastic IP the ssh alias keeps working after a stop and start
Security group inbound tcp/22 from your own addresses only every other service (Orca 6768, Temporal, the bridge) is reached through ssh
Packages git, unison (apt, 2.52 or newer, at /usr/bin/unison; the laptop's Homebrew build may be newer, e.g. 2.54 against the devbox's 2.53: any two versions from 2.52 on work together), Claude Code in ~/.local/bin/claude the sync calls /usr/bin/unison on the devbox; the dream calls claude -p

Sizing guide (AWS us-west-2 on-demand Linux prices, read 2026-09-30; compute is not billed while the instance is stopped, the disk is):

Type vCPU RAM GiB ≈ $/month 24×7 Good for
m7i.2xlarge 8 32 290 the brain + 1–2 agents with tests (the minimum)
m7i.4xlarge 16 64 581 3–4 agents
m7i.8xlarge 32 128 1,161 the reference setup: many agents and heavy builds
gp3 disk — — 0.08 per GB-month 600 GB ≈ $48/month, billed while stopped

Stay on x86_64: a Graviton type (m7g, c7g, r7g) cannot boot an x86 disk.

The ssh alias. On the laptop, add a block to ~/.ssh/config. The name is your devbox_host setting.

Host <devbox-host>
  HostName <elastic-ip>
  User <devbox-user>
  IdentityFile ~/.ssh/<your-key>
  ServerAliveInterval 30
  ServerAliveCountMax 3

On the devbox, let sshd drop dead clients within 3 minutes, so a dead tunnel frees its port by itself. Put this in /etc/ssh/sshd_config.d/10-devbox.conf and reload sshd:

ClientAliveInterval 60
ClientAliveCountMax 3

Check: ssh -o BatchMode=yes <devbox-host> 'uname -sm; nproc; free -g | head -2; df -h ~ | tail -1' prints Linux x86_64, ≥ 8, ≥ 32 GB and ≥ 200 GB without asking for a password.

2. The bind mount: why paths must match

In plain words. The devbox shows its own home folder a second time at your laptop's home path. Then /Users/<user>/brain/notes/x.md is a real path on BOTH machines, so anything that stores an absolute path stays valid on either one.

 devbox disk:   /home/<devbox-user>/brain/notes/x.md
                        ║  bind mount (same folder, second name)
 devbox path:   /Users/<user>/brain/notes/x.md   ◄── the spelling every stored path uses
 laptop path:   /Users/<user>/brain/notes/x.md   ◄── same string
What stores an absolute path What breaks without the mount
Claude Code transcript folders (named after the session's folder) and memory keys a session moved to the devbox starts with no history and no memory
the brain's index, session notes, evidence links every link written on one machine dangles on the other
hook commands in settings.json, the mod, the worker's units hooks point at a binary path that does not exist
Orca worktrees and agent folders brain agents move and resume cannot find the folder

How it is made (scripts/setup-devbox.sh does this, with sudo):

/etc/fstab:   /home/<devbox-user> /Users/<user> none bind,nofail 0 0
sudo mkdir -p /Users/<user> && sudo mount /Users/<user>

Check:

$ findmnt -n -o TARGET /Users/<user>
/Users/<user>
$ test "$(stat -c %i /home/<devbox-user>)" = "$(stat -c %i /Users/<user>)" && echo same-folder
same-folder

Rules that follow from it.

  • Start agents and register Orca projects from /Users/<user>/…, never from /home/<devbox-user>/…. Two spellings split Claude Code's memory keys and transcript folders.
  • Never mv a big tree from one spelling to the other: the kernel sees two mounts, rename() fails with EXDEV, and mv silently copies and deletes instead (LESSONS.md).
  • Remove a git worktree from the same spelling it was registered under.

3. orca serve and pairing

[HUMAN] Installing Orca and pairing it with the laptop app need you.

Install. Put the Orca Linux AppImage at /opt/orca/orca-linux.AppImage (root-owned, executable), from Orca's official release. On Linux outside an Orca terminal, the CLI is orca-ide; a bare orca may be another program.

Run it as a user service. The repository ships deploy/systemd/orca-serve.service (rendered by setup-devbox.sh):

[Service]
WorkingDirectory=/Users/<user>
Environment=LIBGL_ALWAYS_SOFTWARE=1
ExecStart=/opt/orca/orca-linux.AppImage serve --port 6768 --pairing-address 127.0.0.1:16768 --json
Restart=on-failure

systemctl --user daemon-reload && systemctl --user enable --now orca-serve
sudo loginctl enable-linger <devbox-user>      # user services keep running with nobody logged in

Check: systemctl --user is-active orca-serve prints active; loginctl show-user <devbox-user> -p Linger prints Linger=yes.

Why port 16768. The laptop's own Orca runtime already listens on 127.0.0.1:6768, so the laptop forwards 127.0.0.1:16768 to the devbox's 6768, and the server advertises that address in its pairing link.

The laptop tunnel. scripts/setup-laptop.sh installs and loads it as the LaunchAgent com.saahil.orca-devbox-tunnel (KeepAlive, so it comes back after sleep; log ~/Library/Logs/orca-devbox-tunnel.log) and checks that 127.0.0.1:16768 answers. It runs:

/usr/bin/ssh -N -o ExitOnForwardFailure=yes -o ServerAliveInterval=30 -o BatchMode=yes \
    -L 16768:127.0.0.1:6768 <devbox-host>

Pair. The server prints its pairing link once at start, and that line does not reach the journal. Mint it by hand:

  1. On the devbox: systemctl --user stop orca-serve.
  2. In a devbox terminal: script -q -f -c '/opt/orca/orca-linux.AppImage serve --port 6768 --pairing-address 127.0.0.1:16768 --json' ~/orca-pair.log
  3. Copy the orca://pair?code=… link from the output.
  4. On the laptop: orca environment add --name <devbox-host>-server --pairing-code '<link>' (or add the environment in the Orca app).
  5. On the devbox: stop the foreground server (Ctrl+C), delete ~/orca-pair.log (it holds a pairing secret), then systemctl --user start orca-serve.
  6. On the laptop: orca environment list --json. The new environment's id is your orca_env setting.

Register projects on the devbox server with the laptop spelling of the path (in an Orca terminal on the devbox):

orca repo add --path /Users/<user>/Documents/<work-repo>      # your work_repo
orca repo add --path /Users/<user>/Documents/saahil-brain     # your brain_repo (the daily care agent needs it)

Check: the laptop's Orca app shows the devbox environment connected and both projects listed.

4. Tunnels

Every connection between the machines rides on ssh. Nothing listens on a public port.

Tunnel Command shape Started by What uses it
Orca laptop ssh -N -L 127.0.0.1:16768:127.0.0.1:6768 <devbox-host> com.saahil.orca-devbox-tunnel (setup-laptop.sh) the laptop Orca app → orca serve
brain bridge laptop ssh -N -R 127.0.0.1:7722:127.0.0.1:7722 <devbox-host> com.saahil.brain-tunnel (brain bridge install) the devbox → the laptop's brain bridge (mesh, peer steps, sync)
sync laptop ssh <devbox-host> running /usr/bin/unison com.saahil.brain-sync, brain sync Unison
Temporal UI laptop ssh -N -L 8233:127.0.0.1:8233 <devbox-host> you, when you want the UI http://127.0.0.1:8233/namespaces/brain/workflows

Why the laptop dials out. A company-managed Mac has its ssh server off by policy, and turning on Remote Login does not start it. The devbox therefore cannot ssh into the laptop. The laptop opens every connection; the reverse forward (-R) is how the devbox talks back, and only to the token-checked bridge on the laptop's loopback.

If a tunnel is down: launchctl kickstart -k gui/$(id -u)/com.saahil.brain-tunnel on the laptop, and read ~/Library/Logs/brain-tunnel.log. A stale 7722 listener on the devbox clears by itself within 3 minutes (section 1, sshd keepalive).

5. The devbox helper

scripts/devbox is a small laptop script that controls the instance through the AWS EC2 API. setup-laptop.sh installs it as ~/.local/bin/devbox. brain machine up|down|status|sync on the laptop run this same script.

Command Does
devbox up start the instance (~1–2 min), wait for ssh, run brain sync
devbox status instance state, uptime and load, GitHub certificate expiry, AWS SSO state
devbox sync brain sync
devbox down [--force] refuse while heavy processes (go test, kubectl, depot) or Claude sessions run; else brain sync, then stop the instance

It reads three optional keys from ~/.config/brain/identity.json: devbox_instance_id, devbox_region and devbox_aws_profile (region and profile fall back to the AWS CLI defaults); see CONFIG.md. setup-devbox.sh fills the instance id and region from the EC2 instance metadata, and the profile from its --aws-profile flag.

Guards that must stay.

  • down refuses while work runs. Stopping the instance ends every agent on it; transcripts survive, and brain agents resume <name> <session> brings one back.
  • A failed instance-state read is fatal: the helper names the sign-in to renew and exits 1. It never prints a blank "already" (LESSONS.md).
  • Test down with a stub aws on PATH, never against the real instance.

6. Sign-ins

Sign-in Lifetime Renew Symptom when it lapses
GitHub (SSH certificate, github_cert) hours (company flow) brain machine login github, or your team's flow git push: Permission denied (publickey)
AWS SSO (aws_sso_session) the SSO session length brain machine login aws devbox up/status: Token has expired; brain machine status shows it
gcloud until Google asks again brain machine login gcloud Reauthentication required
Claude (for the dream's model calls) persistent sign in to Claude Code on the devbox with your own login; the brain-worker unit sets BRAIN_LLM_LOGIN=1 so the dream uses it, no API key (CONFIG.md) dream steps fail with an auth error in .brain/dream-runs/

brain machine login drives the same sign-in helpers as your team's devbox setup. Each sign-in is a browser flow: [HUMAN].

7. Security

  • No public ports. Orca's 6768 listens on all interfaces (it has no bind flag), so the security group must keep it closed; reach it through the ssh forward only. setup-devbox.sh probes the devbox's public address and warns if 6768 answers there.
  • The bridge listens only on the laptop's 127.0.0.1, needs the token, answers an allow-list of named steps, and logs every request without its text. It is not a shell.
  • Temporal and its UI bind to the devbox's 127.0.0.1. The brain's Temporal is local and personal; never point it at a company Temporal Cloud account.
  • Brain data (docs, notes, sessions) never leaves the two machines, except as input to model API calls, as every agent session already does.
